results.method: Re-ran the deterministic builtin detector at its native operating point over the cached labelled rows of each registry slice (cache SHA-256 verified against the registry record first; row counts verified against the registry). Human FPR = P(verdict=ai_like | human); native TPR = P(verdict=ai_like | AI) at the same operating point. Intervals are Wilson 95% CIs (z=1.96) from the re-run (k, n) counts. The registry's bootstrap fpr_native CIs are all the degenerate [0.0, 0.0] (a percentile bootstrap over an all-zero sample cannot resample a positive); Wilson is the honest interval here and replaces nothing in the registry — see the companion registry-patch recommendation.

notes:
Pooling is NOT legitimate as the gate statistic. The slices differ in regime (raw vs human-edited), language (en vs mul 8-language vs en+de), domain, generator vintage and editing; pooling hides that heterogeneity, and the segment slice is a different unit (sentences, not documents) that must never be pooled with document slices at all. The pooled numbers are reported for completeness only. The release gate must use the per-slice worst Wilson ci_upper among the document slices that meet the sample minimum — a single pooled number would let a large slice (DetectRL-X, n=400) mask a thin slice (OpAI-Bench 20261106, n=56, Wilson upper 0.0642).

Still unknown:
- Worst-slice human FPR as a *supported* claim: no slice is supported (all records are unreviewed partial seeds), and two document slices fail the FPR bar outright (OpAI-Bench 20261106: n=56, Wilson upper above the 0.05 ceiling; RAID: n=92, below the 100-human minimum). The report-card lead ('worst-slice human FPR = unknown') changes only by a parent decision; this artifact does not change it.
- Human FPR on slices the registry does not cover at all: non-English document text outside DetectRL-X/GhostWriter, ESL human text, texts below 80 words, generators newer than each record's declared vintage, and human populations outside the declared ones.
- Whether the zero observed false positives persist on larger human samples: every Wilson upper bound here is a bound on zero events, not a measured positive rate. A larger human sample (RAID growth is worker 1's parallel work) could produce the first false positive and move the bound.
- Per-language / per-domain / per-generator FPR: this re-run reports one pooled slice per dataset, as the registry does; finer slices are wave-2 work.

This artifact re-expresses EV-20261108-human-fpr in run-artifact/v1 shape with every measured value unchanged. It is not a new claim and it does not change the report-card lead: the gate reads results["worst_slice_human_fpr"] for the lead, and this artifact deliberately carries no such key — 0.0642 is the Wilson 95% upper bound on a 0/56 rate (OpAI-Bench 20261106), not a measured FPR point rate. No claim cites this record; the worst-slice human FPR as a supported claim remains unknown.
